channel.title: Manuel Castillejo Blog
channel.description: Reporting and analysis on cognitive health, emerging technology and artificial intelligence.

item.title: Offline Work Should Be a Planned Mode, Not an Emergency Workaround.
item.description: Nextcloud's new desktop download separates local editing from connected collaboration. Teams can use that distinction to prepare work that remains useful without a live connection.

item.title: Keep a Creative Role Before the AI Draft Arrives.
item.description: New reporting on a creative-writing experiment highlights a useful distinction: approving an AI draft is not the same as shaping the idea it develops.

item.title: Cross-Team Practice Needs a Home Outside the Project Plan.
item.description: CNCF's new User Group Program separates enduring domains from bounded initiatives. For teams, the useful question is where shared problems belong when no single project owns them.

item.title: Before Changing How a Team Works, Name What Would Prove You Wrong.
item.description: Stefan Thomke's new book puts untested management assumptions in view. Treat a proposed workflow change as a claim to examine, not a rule to defend.

item.title: Sharing an AI Skill Is Not Updating a Team Standard.
item.description: Google's new Workspace skills rollout makes reusable AI instructions easier to distribute. Teams still need a maintenance route when shared instructions become independent copies.

item.title: When Priorities Change, Give Your AI the Work to Stop.
item.description: New coverage of Perplexity Teammates puts ongoing AI work in view. Teams need a deliberate handoff when priorities change, including which previous instructions no longer apply.

item.title: Before Reading the AI Adoption Chart, Check What It Cannot See.
item.description: GitHub's new Copilot reporting fields expose missing telemetry and outdated clients. The management lesson is to distinguish unobserved activity from inactivity before drawing conclusions about a team.

item.title: Use AI to Find the Work That Should Not Arrive.
item.description: New coverage of Gartner's customer-service research suggests a different productivity question: can AI help teams identify recurring problems that create unnecessary work, rather than only handle that work faster?

item.title: An AI Workflow Should Recover Without Doing the Work Twice.
item.description: Mistral's new Studio release puts durable execution in view. Teams need to test whether automation can recover from a lost confirmation without creating duplicate work.

item.title: Time Flexibility Needs a Decision Right, Not Just a Remote Day.
item.description: New British Social Attitudes findings reveal a gap between valuing control over working hours and having it. Teams should define which scheduling choices people can actually make, not treat remote access as sufficient flexibility.

item.title: An AI Agent Can Be Authorized and Still Be Wrong.
item.description: CrowdStrike's proposed Fiddler acquisition highlights a distinction teams need to preserve: legitimate access does not establish that an automated action was the right business decision.

item.title: Rehearse the Coordination Before the Work Becomes Consequential.
item.description: Purdue's new account of a classroom escape-room exercise suggests a practical team-design lesson: test how people coordinate on a harmless task before relying on the process for consequential work.

item.title: AI Should Shorten the Work Route, Not Add Another Stop.
item.description: New coverage of ActivTrak's research highlights differences between embedded and browser-based AI. The practical question is how many unnecessary round trips a tool adds to an ordinary task.

item.title: Availability Is Not Engagement. Stop Managing Them as One Thing.
item.description: HBR's new review of falling U.S. employee engagement is a reason to examine the relationship with work, not demand more visible activity. Async teams need service commitments without permanent availability.

item.title: AI Changes the Cost of Work Before It Changes the Price.
item.description: A new Florida Bar resource highlights a small-firm survey in which reported AI efficiency outpaces pricing changes. The practical lesson is to cost the complete service before deciding what faster work is worth.

item.title: Standardize the Security. Let People Configure the Work.
item.description: Logitech's October 28 commentary revisits research on technology control. The practical lesson is to distinguish necessary workplace safeguards from defaults that people should be able to change.

item.title: Recurring Coordination Should Have an Expiry Date.
item.description: Fedora's Community Ops team has discontinued its recurring general meetings while keeping project-specific calls available. The useful lesson is to give intensive coordination an end condition, not a permanent calendar slot.

item.title: Your AI Supplier's Worker Data Belongs in the Procurement Review.
item.description: New privacy complaints about Scale AI's Outlier platform highlight an overlooked procurement question: what must the people behind an AI service disclose to do their work?

item.title: Before Buying Better Meeting AI, Check Who the Room Can Hear.
item.description: Shure's newly announced IDC recognition puts speech capture beside meeting AI. The practical lesson is to test listening conditions across the room before trusting the automated record.

item.title: Your Team's Average Delivery Time Is Hiding a Different Problem.
item.description: Google Sheets' new box and whisker charts make variation easier to inspect. For teams, the useful lesson is to examine how reliably work moves, not just whether the average looks faster.

item.title: Before an AI Rollout, Agree on How the Job Will Change.
item.description: A new Danish labour-market policy study puts worker involvement beside AI adoption. For teams, the practical lesson is to negotiate changes to responsibilities and expectations before a pilot quietly becomes the new job.

item.title: An AI Agent Should Not Be Able to Rewrite Its Own Oversight.
item.description: New reporting on OpenAI's internal monitoring incidents exposes a practical boundary for AI-assisted work: permission to complete a task is not permission to weaken the controls around it.

item.title: Arc Is Shutting Down. Your Work Setup Should Be Able to Leave.
item.description: The Browser Company's October 22 announcement gives Arc users a migration deadline. It also offers a practical lesson for teams: evaluate productivity tools by how well a working setup survives the exit, not only how convenient it feels inside.

item.title: AI Makes Work Look Finished. Performance Reviews Need a Better Standard.
item.description: A newly released monday.com survey finds that more than half of senior leaders struggle to evaluate AI-assisted work. The useful response is to assess demonstrated judgment, not guess who wrote each sentence.

item.title: Workplace AI Needs Context. Teams Need to Know Which Context to Trust.
item.description: Zoom's new Unified Context Layer is built around a real workplace problem: decisions disappear across meetings, chats and systems. The management opportunity is not to collect more history, but to make the right context attributable, current and actionable.

item.title: AI Access Is a Work Design Problem Before It Is an AI Problem.
item.description: The World Bank Group's new digital strategy puts a neglected condition ahead of the AI headline: people need affordable access, relevant services and usable skills before technology can improve how work gets done.

item.title: When AI Produces More Work, Attention Becomes the System Constraint.
item.description: New internal research from Anthropic shows a workplace where agent output can exceed a person's capacity to review it. The management task is to design queues, thresholds and decision rights before faster production becomes faster interruption.

item.title: AI Is Taking Junior Tasks. Teams Need to Redesign How Expertise Is Learned.
item.description: A new Oliver Wyman Forum report finds AI is already doing some tasks junior employees once learned from managers. The management task is not to preserve busywork, but to make the path from assisted work to independent judgment visible.

item.title: AI Can Answer the Question. Teams Still Need to Know Who Knows the Work.
item.description: A new survey of 1,033 U.S. desk workers raises a useful coordination question: when AI replaces a colleague as the first place to ask, teams can lose sight of the expertise they need to rely on.

item.title: AI Can Compare the Scenarios. Teams Still Have to Own the Trade-Off.
item.description: Workday's newly announced Decision Intelligence product points to a useful management discipline: faster scenario analysis only improves work when assumptions, authority and outcomes remain visible.

item.title: AI Does Not Fix Meetings. It Raises the Standard for Them.
item.description: Jabra's new WorkLife 2026 survey reports that more work is expanding even as AI enters daily routines. The practical response is to make meetings accountable decision points, not cheaper containers for more activity.

item.title: When AI Joins the Conversation, Governance Must Follow the Thread.
item.description: A newly reported financial-services survey points to a practical workplace AI problem: control is not about preserving every prompt, but retaining the context needed to review consequential work.

item.title: The Useful AI Metric Is Not Answers Delivered. It Is Escalations Avoided.
item.description: Microsoft's latest HR account points to a more useful workplace AI test: whether a system makes routine work legible while preserving a clear route to human judgment.

item.title: AI Can Speed Up Work. It Cannot Protect Deep Work for You.
item.description: New workplace data show that AI can improve task productivity. The harder question for teams is whether the time gained becomes better work or simply more interruption.

item.title: AI May Spot Cognitive Decline Earlier. The Hard Part Starts After the Signal.
item.description: The NIH's 2026 progress report highlights StateViewer, a tool combining PET imaging and AI to support earlier detection. The point is not to outsource clinical judgment, but to design the next step better.
